description:
We are conducting researches independently from the datas of NASA missions. For "Flame in Freefall," we're analyzing NASA microgravity data to build an intelligent fire safety dashboard predicting space flame dynamics.

​Why join? Deep scientific grounding, clear execution, and a high-impact vision.

​Let’s build something incredible!
summary:
Fire behaves differently in space. Without buoyancy, flames become spherical, burn at lower temperatures, can sustain “cool flame” chemistry, and may persist or extinguish under conditions that would be unremarkable on Earth. Yet spacecraft fire-safety practice still leans heavily on normal-gravity testing. This project delivers the Spacecraft Fire Safety Scientific Inference (SI) Engine, a web application that unifies NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion datasets from FLEX, ACME, SAME, SAFFIRE, SPICE, BASS, DAFT and related experiments into one searchable, quantitative framework.

Users enter mission conditions: oxygen concentration, total pressure, gravity level, diluent gas, ambient flow velocity, material or fuel, and sample size. The engine saves each scenario, cross-references it against the experimental records, and computes a Fire Safety Index with confidence bounds. It estimates ignition susceptibility, flame-spread tendency, extinction likelihood, and the most plausible flame regime: hot, warm, cool or oscillatory. Every result cites its supporting experiments and flags any extrapolation beyond measured data.

By sorting heterogeneous results onto shared metrics, the app lets engineers compare habitats, from the ISS to lunar and Martian systems, and find where fire risk is unexpectedly high or low. It is a research decision-support tool, not a certified safety authority.
details:
The project involves the creation of an SI engine whose express purpose is to accept environmental metrics of space mission scenarios as the input, cross-reference them with experimental data and information parsed from actual research papers, analyze them and provide a real-time educated estimate on the risk of flame threat for that specific environment as the output.

The SI engine is powered by an AI agent, operated under strict guidelines, in order to analyze the given scenario. The agent uses statistical techniques such as kernel weighting and ridge regression to make the most of the limited research data available in this field, and also having access to its normal science database in order to draw logical steps to extrapolate if needed, while still remaining constrained by the verified research datasets. The engine then scores each environmental metric given, and the final fire safety rating is calculated from their weighted sum. A 'Confidence' rating is also issued to quantify how close the analyzed scenario is to the information in the dataset, thereby informing the user how much, or how little, the agent has extrapolated conclusions of its own.

Several quality of life features have also been implemented, including the ability to save analyzed scenarios for future reference, built-in presets of commonly studied mission scenarios (such as the environment in the ISS, or on the moon), a built-in database of the experimental data extracted from the research papers housed within the software itself, as well as an experimental 'Sensor Agent' capable of automatically syncing and recording physical data from external sensors aboard spacecraft, reporting risk immediately, thereby opening up the pathway for complete automation where the user would not have to measure and enter the mission conditions to the SI engine on their own.

The project is intended to further the endeavor to create predictive tools to analyze extraterrestrial fire safety in real time. In intensive mission scenarios, astronauts and ground support cannot rely on scattered research studies to determine if an environment is safe or not. Thus, a solution that can produce a quick, concise and reliable measure of fire risk at once is of paramount importance to protect human lives and mission assets in space.

Claude (from Anthropic) was used to extract and parse the data from the research papers. Google AI studio was used to construct the SI engine itself under our detailed parameters.

The SI Engine has potential beyond its current form. It was built in Google AI Studio, and its core computation runs in the browser by design, so the code can later be exported and deployed locally or as a standalone web app. Only the AI-written narrative requires a Gemini API key, supplied by the deployer and ideally held on a server rather than in client code. Any AI Studio–specific storage would need to be replaced with the deployer’s own.
